title: Chain Rule, Work and Wages

references.label: GSSSB Laboratory Assistant Detailed Syllabus, Part A (Advt. 327/2025-26)

scientificNotes: General competitive-exam quantitative-aptitude topic; included to match the exam's Part A scope.
expression: For direct variation: more of A → more of B, in same proportion. For inverse variation: more of A → less of B, in reciprocal proportion. Combined chain: (product of one set of quantities) / (product of corresponding quantities) held in fixed proportion.
explanation: The CHAIN RULE generalises simple proportion to problems with MULTIPLE varying quantities linked together (e.g. workers, days, hours per day, and units of work, all changing simultaneously) — set up each pairwise relationship as either DIRECT variation (both quantities increase/decrease together, e.g. more workers → more work done in the same time) or INVERSE variation (one increases as the other decreases, e.g. more workers → FEWER days needed for the same work), then combine all the ratios into one equation and solve for the unknown. WAGES problems apply the same logic: wages earned are usually directly proportional to (number of workers) × (number of days worked) × (hours worked per day) for identical work — so if the total work and total wage pool are fixed, individual wage share follows the same 'capital-time'-style proportional split used in partnership problems, just substituting labour-time for capital-time.

variables.meaning: Number of people/units doing the work
Amount of work completed (often normalised to 1 job or given as a numeric quantity)

workedExample.scenario: 12 workers can complete a job in 8 days working 6 hours/day. How many days will 16 workers take, working 8 hours/day, for the SAME job?

commonMistakes: Treating every quantity in a chain-rule problem as directly proportional — some relationships (like workers vs. days needed, for fixed total work) are INVERSELY proportional, and mislabelling the direction inverts the final answer.

Forgetting that when EFFICIENCY differs between workers (some problems specify one worker does 'twice the work' of another), a straight headcount ratio must instead be replaced with an efficiency-weighted ratio.
genZNote: Chain rule is just proportion problems that decided to bring three or four friends along instead of coming solo — nail down direct vs inverse for EACH pair before combining.
